questions.q: What is the core principle of Zero Trust?
options: Never grant trust based on network location alone — verify every request explicitly, every time
Trust any device once it connects to the corporate VPN
Trust anything inside the firewall and scrutinize only external traffic
Zero Trust means disabling all authentication to simplify access
questions.explain: Zero Trust verifies every request explicitly, regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the traditional network perimeter.

options: A strong perimeter defense where anything already inside the firewall is implicitly trusted
A model where every request is verified individually, regardless of location
A cloud-native security pattern introduced alongside Zero Trust
A type of encryption used for data at rest
questions.explain: Castle-and-moat relies on a strong perimeter (the firewall); once inside, traffic was historically trusted with little further scrutiny.

questions.q: What two developments made the castle-and-moat model stop working?
options: Remote work and cloud adoption, which moved users and resources outside the traditional network perimeter
Faster internet speeds and cheaper hardware
The invention of the firewall itself
A decrease in the number of cyberattacks
questions.explain: Remote work meant users connected from untrusted networks, and cloud adoption meant resources lived outside the on-prem perimeter — leaving no single boundary to defend.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three core Zero Trust tenets described in this lesson?
options: Assume breach — design and monitor as if an attacker is already inside
Trust by default — assume every internal request is safe
Perimeter-only verification — check identity once at the network edge
Ignore device health when evaluating a sign-in
questions.explain: Zero Trust frameworks commonly rest on verify explicitly, least privilege access, and assume breach.

questions.q: Under Zero Trust, what role does network location play in an access decision?
options: It's one signal among several, but never by itself a reason to skip verification
It's the only factor that matters — inside the network means automatic access
It is completely irrelevant and never evaluated at all
It replaces the need for identity verification entirely
questions.explain: Zero Trust still considers location as one signal, but it never substitutes for explicit verification of the request itself.
